summary: Defines the Session Description Protocol, a text format for describing multimedia sessions for announcement, invitation and other forms of session initiation. It is widely used with SIP and RTP. It was standards-track and has been replaced by RFC 8866.

eli5.summary: SDP is like the info card for a phone or video call. It lists what kinds of sound and picture will be sent and where to send them.

questions: what is the o= line in sdp
subtitle: A compact text format for describing who, what, where and when of a multimedia session.

tldr.problem: People starting a call, stream or multicast conference need a standard way to tell each other the media, addresses, ports and times involved, no matter how that information is delivered.
tldr.mechanism: SDP is a plain-text format of one-letter type=value lines in a fixed order, split into a session-level part and one or more media-level parts, with attributes (a=) as the extension mechanism.
tldr.outcome: SDP describes a session but does not carry it or negotiate it. RFC 4566 was obsoleted by RFC 8866.

today: RFC 4566 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 8866, which is the current definition of SDP. It itself replaced RFC 2327 and RFC 3266.

sections.title: What SDP Is For
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) gives a standard representation for the details needed to join a multimedia session: media details, transport addresses and other metadata. It is purely a format. It does not include a transport protocol and can be carried by the Session Announcement Protocol, the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), the Real Time Streaming Protocol, email using MIME, or HTTP.

SDP is deliberately general purpose, but it is not meant to negotiate session content or media encodings. That is outside the scope of session description. The RFC gives examples of use: SIP messages carry session descriptions so participants can agree on compatible media types, RTSP uses SDP syntax to describe delivery parameters, and a distributed session directory can periodically announce multicast sessions to a well-known multicast group. Over email or the web the media type application/sdp is used.

A session description conveys the session name and purpose, the times it is active, the media in it, and what is needed to receive that media (addresses, ports, formats). Optionally it adds bandwidth and contact information.
sections.eli5: SDP is just the invitation card. It says what the party is, when it is and where to go. It does not drive you there.

sections.title: Lines, Order and Sections
sections.content:
An SDP description is entirely text, using UTF-8. The text form was chosen for portability and flexible toolkits, while the encoding is kept compact. Strict order and formatting rules mean most damage to an announcement makes it malformed and easy to discard.

Every line has the form <type>=<value>. The type is exactly one case-significant character, and whitespace MUST NOT appear on either side of the =. A description has a session-level section that starts with v=, followed by zero or more media-level sections, each starting with m=. Session-level values are the default for all media unless a media-level value overrides them.

Lines must appear in the order the RFC gives. The required ones are v= (version), o= (origin), s= (session name) and at least one t= (timing). Optional ones include i=, u=, e=, p=, c=, b=, r=, z=, k= and a=. Records end with CRLF, though parsers SHOULD also accept a single newline.

The set of type letters is deliberately small and not extensible. A parser MUST completely ignore a description containing a type letter it does not understand. Extension happens through attributes instead, and a parser MUST ignore any attribute it does not understand.
sections.eli5: Each line of the card starts with one letter and an equals sign, like s= for the name. The lines must come in the same order every time, so a reader can spot a smudged card right away.

sections.title: The Main Fields
sections.content:
The v= line gives the SDP version. This memo defines version 0, and there is no minor version. The o= line names the originator: username, a session id, a session version, a network type (IN for Internet), an address type (IP4 or IP6) and the address of the creating host. Together these identify the session, and the version must increase when the description is modified. The s= line is the session name; it MUST NOT be empty, and s= (a single space) is used if there is no meaningful name.

The c= line holds connection data: network type, address type and connection address. A description MUST have either one c= line in each media description or a single one at session level. For IPv4 multicast a time to live (TTL) in the range 0-255 MUST be given after a slash, as in c=IN IP4 224.2.36.42/127, though TTL scoping is deprecated in favour of administratively scoped addresses. IPv6 multicast MUST NOT carry a TTL.

The t= line gives start and stop times as decimal NTP seconds since 1900. A stop time of zero means the session is unbounded, and zero for both means permanent; user interfaces SHOULD strongly discourage those. The r= line adds repeat times, for example r=7d 1h 0 25h for a weekly session with two slots. Monthly and yearly repeats cannot be expressed with one repeat line.

The m= line starts a media description: m=<media> <port> <proto> <fmt> .... Defined media are audio, video, text, application and message. For RTP/AVP and RTP/SAVP the formats are RTP payload type numbers, and the first listed is the default. The b= line proposes bandwidth in kilobits per second by default, with CT (conference total) and AS (application specific) defined.

Other optional lines: i= free-text information, u= a URI for more detail, e= and p= contact details (both optional in this version), and z= time zone adjustments.
sections.eli5: The card names who made it, what it is called, where to send the sound and picture, and when it runs. Each kind of media, like audio or video, gets its own small block.

sections.title: Attributes
sections.content:
An a= line is the primary way to extend SDP. It can be a property (a=recvonly) or a value (a=orient:landscape). Attributes before the first m= line are session-level and apply to the whole conference. Attributes after it are media-level. A receiver MUST ignore an attribute it does not understand.

Section 6 defines a starting set. a=rtpmap maps an RTP payload type number to an encoding name, clock rate and optional parameters, for example a=rtpmap:98 L16/16000/2 for a dynamic type. a=fmtp passes format-specific parameters through without SDP needing to understand them. a=ptime and a=maxptime give packet time in milliseconds.

The direction attributes sendrecv, sendonly, recvonly and inactive say how tools should start. If none is present, sendrecv SHOULD be assumed except for "broadcast" or "H332" conferences. Others cover category (cat), keywords (keywds), tool name (tool), orientation, conference type, character set (charset), languages (sdplang, lang), framerate and quality.
sections.eli5: Extra sticky notes can be added to the card, like "listen only" or "video, please". If a reader does not know a note, it simply skips it.

sections.title: Security and Registration
sections.content:
A session description cannot be trusted unless it was obtained over an authenticated transport from a known, trusted source. Otherwise the media may not be the intended ones, the destination may be wrong, or media security may be compromised. Software that parses a description MUST NOT be able to start anything other than specifically configured multimedia software. A description arriving by announcement, email, invitation or web page MUST NOT put the user into an interactive session unless the user pre-authorised it.

The k= line conveys an encryption key in the clear, with no way to name the algorithm and room for only one key. Its use is NOT RECOMMENDED, and SDP MUST NOT carry key material unless the channel is both private and authenticated. Intermediaries that read or rewrite SDP, such as to open firewall holes or follow NAT bindings, are NOT RECOMMENDED unless the authenticity and authority of the description can be checked.

For IANA, the RFC updates the application/sdp media type and defines registries for seven names: media, proto, fmt, attribute names, bwtype, nettype and addrtype. Attribute names MUST be registered. The old enckey table is obsolete and new registrations MUST NOT be accepted. Section 9 gives an ABNF grammar.
sections.eli5: A card from a stranger might lie, so do not just follow it. Never write a secret password on the card, because anyone along the way can read it.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 2327
sections.content:
RFC 4566 obsoletes RFC 2327 and RFC 3266. It adds a media type registration for SDP, tightens registration requirements, and notes that text and message are valid media while control and data are deprecated. It registers the RTP/SAVP profile and adds the attributes a=inactive and a=maxptime.

Both e= and p= became optional to match actual usage. The limits of k= are noted and its use is deprecated, and most uses of the x- prefix for experimental parameters are disallowed.
sections.eli5: This is the new edition of the card design. It fixes a few rules that nobody followed and retires one risky box.

o=jdoe 2890844526 2890842807 IN IP4 10.47.16.5

u=http://www.example.com/seminars/sdp.pdf
